summary: Ages 5–6 (Reception/Year 1) counting objects to 20: coordinating one-to-one correspondence (tag each item exactly once) with cardinality (the last count word is the total) to answer 'how many?' for sets in any arrangement — line, array, circle, or scattered — and to count out a given number (give-N). Scattered sets are hardest because the child must impose a tracking strategy; give-N is the strongest check of cardinality. Ten-frames help teen numbers read as 'ten and some more', seeding place value. (The cited standard specifies scattered configurations up to 10 and ordered arrangements up to 20.)
misconceptions: Losing track on scattered sets → skips or double-counts (no tracking strategy).
Recounting when asked 'how many?' (cardinality not secure) or miscounting across the teens.
Treating teen numbers as unanalysable words rather than 'ten and some ones'.
Believing a rearranged set has a different total (conservation).

activities.title: Organise and count a scattered set
steps: Start with a small scattered pile (up to 10) of moveable counters or buttons spread randomly.
Count them by moving each counted item aside into a 'counted' tray (or sliding it along a consistent path) so counted and uncounted are clearly separated.
Say how many there are altogether, then recount and check you get the same number.
Repeat with a larger scattered set of up to 20 counters (a harder extension), choosing your own tracking path.
Match a numeral card to the final count.
activities.insight: A chaotic scatter becomes reliably countable by imposing order — moving each item as you count it so nothing is skipped or counted twice — and the last number you say is how many there are, no matter how the objects are arranged.

activities.title: Count out exactly N (give-N)
steps: From a large pile, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me 13') into a cupped hand or small tray.
Say the target first, then count one item at a time, stopping when you reach it.
Check: 'How many did we need? Tell me when to stop' — point and count together to confirm you stopped at the target.
Try a round with a teen target such as 16, then compare counting out from different-sized piles.
activities.insight: Counting out a specific quantity means using the target number as a stop signal — you hold the goal in mind while counting, which is cardinality in action and a stronger test than simply reporting 'how many'.

activities.title: Vary the arrangement to make counting robust
steps: Count the same quantity shown four ways in turn: a line, a rectangular array, a circle, and scattered.
After counting a neat line, count it again starting from the other end and check the total is the same.
Count an array along rows, then along columns, and confirm the total does not change.
State each total aloud with 'altogether' and match it to the written numeral.
activities.insight: The total depends only on the objects, not on how they are laid out or which end you start from — a rearranged set still has the same number.

activities.title: Read teen numbers on a ten-frame as 'ten and some more'
steps: Count a teen quantity (11–19) by filling a ten-frame completely first, then placing the extras in a second frame.
Say the number as 'ten and three… thirteen' so the full ten and the extras are both visible.
Match the ten-frame picture to the written numeral (e.g. 13).
Repeat with other teen numbers, each time noticing the full ten plus a few more.
activities.insight: A teen number is not a mysterious word — it is a full ten with a few more ones, which is the beginning of place value.

activities.title: Spot and fix a miscount (optional Socratic check)
steps: Watch (or listen to) a puppet or partner count a scattered pile, deliberately skipping one item or counting one twice.
Decide whether the count was right, explain what went wrong, and show how to count it correctly using a tracking strategy.
Suggest what the puppet should do differently next time (e.g. move each item aside).
activities.insight: Being able to catch and explain a counting slip shows you understand why one-to-one tagging and tracking matter — not just how to recite numbers.

checkQuestion: Here are 17 counters in a line — count them and tell me how many. Now here are 10 counters scattered on the table — count these. Last, here's a big pile: count out exactly 13 for me. (Watch the one-to-one tagging, whether they organise the scattered set, and whether they stop at 13.)
checkAnswer: Tags each object once, keeps track of counted versus uncounted in the scattered set (moving or organising them), answers 'how many' with the last count word, and stops at exactly 13 when counting out.
